Conflict Management Therapy

Conflict Management Therapy helps clients develop practical skills in communication, emotional regulation, and de-escalation so that interpersonal disputes are resolved more safely and constructively. Sessions focus on clear, respectful expression, active listening, boundary-setting, and problem-solving strategies that reduce reactivity and rebuild trust. Michelle Barratt Psychology (MBP) provides in-person therapy across Brisbane, and flexible online therapy options Australia-wide, ensuring that access to support is always accessible.

How does MBP support Conflict Management Therapy?

Michelle Barratt Psychology and Administrative Services (MBP) provides a neutral, professional administrative hub for clients and clinicians in Brisbane and across Australia .

MBP manages scheduling, intake communications, and administrative coordination in an impartial way so that independent Brisbane psychologists and allied practitioners can preserve their clinical objectivity and focus on therapeutic work.

This administrative neutrality helps ensure fairness, confidentiality, and clear communication for all parties involved.

What is Conflict?

Conflict occurs when two or more people have differing needs, expectations, values, perspectives, or goals. While conflict is often viewed negatively, disagreements can also create opportunities for growth, understanding, and positive change when managed effectively.

The challenge is not whether conflict occurs, but how it is handled. Constructive conflict management can strengthen relationships, improve communication, and help people work collaboratively towards solutions

How Conflict Affects Relationships

When conflict becomes ongoing or unresolved, it can place significant strain on relationships. Communication may break down, trust can be damaged, and people may begin to feel unheard, misunderstood, or emotionally disconnected.

Over time, unresolved conflict may contribute to stress, resentment, avoidance, anxiety, and relationship dissatisfaction. Early intervention can help individuals and couples develop healthier ways of communicating and resolving disagreements before conflict becomes deeply entrenched.

Signs of Unhealthy Conflict

Certain patterns can make conflict more difficult to resolve and may contribute to ongoing relationship distress. Common examples include criticism, defensiveness, contempt, avoidance, emotional withdrawal, blame, and an unwillingness to consider another person's perspective.

These patterns often develop gradually and can become entrenched over time. Therapy helps individuals and couples recognise these behaviours, understand their impact, and develop more effective communication and problem-solving strategies.

What is Conflict Resolution Therapy?

Conflict resolution therapy provides a structured and supportive environment where individuals, couples, or families can explore disagreements, improve communication, and work towards mutually beneficial outcomes.

Rather than focusing solely on who is right or wrong, therapy helps participants understand each other's perspectives, identify underlying concerns, develop empathy, and strengthen problem-solving skills. The goal is to build healthier relationship patterns and improve the ability to manage future disagreements constructively.

When Should You Seek Support?

Many people seek conflict management therapy when they find themselves having the same disagreements repeatedly, struggling to communicate effectively, feeling emotionally disconnected, or experiencing ongoing tension in their relationships.

Seeking support early can prevent conflict from escalating and provide practical tools for improving communication, managing emotions, and restoring healthier relationship dynamics.

When Conflict Resolution Therapy May Not Be Appropriate

Conflict resolution therapy relies on all parties being able to participate safely, voluntarily, and respectfully. In situations involving domestic violence, coercive control, abuse, intimidation, or significant safety concerns, joint conflict resolution or couples therapy may not be appropriate.

Where abuse is present or suspected, individual support and specialised services are generally recommended before any form of joint therapy is considered. Client safety and wellbeing must always remain the priority.

The absence of conflict does not define healthy relationships; rather, it is the ability to work through disagreements respectfully and constructively. With the right support, individuals, couples, and families can develop stronger communication skills and more positive relationship patterns.

Building Healthier Relationships Through Better Communication

Conflict affects more than the individuals directly involved. Ongoing disagreements can influence family relationships, parenting, emotional wellbeing, and the overall atmosphere within a household.

Learning healthier communication and conflict resolution skills can strengthen relationships, reduce stress, and improve understanding between partners, family members, and loved ones.

Therapy provides a supportive environment where people can learn practical strategies for navigating disagreements while maintaining respect, empathy, and connection.

1 Effective Communication

Learn skills that promote understanding and reduce misunderstandings.

2 Emotional Awareness

Recognise emotions and respond more thoughtfully during conflict.

3 Active Listening

Develop the ability to listen openly and understand different perspectives.

4 Problem Solving

Build practical strategies for resolving disagreements constructively.

5 Healthy Boundaries

Establish respectful boundaries that support positive relationships.
